learn.intro: Jev reads the words you give it, literally. That is a strength, and a risk: wording can hide the real meaning, point at someone else, or even try to give Jev orders. Here are six messages, each written plainly and then in a tricky way. Guess which tricks fool Jev, then see what really happened.

compare.title: Jev
points: Answers the exact question it was asked
Can be misled by tricky phrasing

compare.title: An LLM
points: Reads the whole message in context
Its answer can come back in the wrong format

tasks.title: Twelve messages: six plain, six tricky

why: Most tricks did not fool Jev: it read negations, other people and planted orders correctly. Where it slipped, the probability was close to the middle, a sign it was unsure.
Literal reading means the question must be precise. Ask exactly what you need to know, and treat any text you did not write as data, never as instructions.
These items were rewritten once after a first set did not fool Jev at all. Both results are on the Methodology page.

questions.prompt: How do you make Jev harder to trick?

options.text: Ask a precise question and treat user text as data

questions.explanation: Precise questions leave less room for wording to mislead, and text from users should never be followed as an order.

questions.prompt: What was a sign that Jev might be wrong on a trick?
questions.explanation: A probability near 50 percent means Jev was unsure, which is the cue to review the item.
